question: How did my phone-drawer focus plan change?

retrieval.warning: Exact quotations prove provenance, not semantic support.

evidence.title: 2026-06-10-focus-plan
evidence.quote:
# Focus plan, June 10

I thought putting my phone in a drawer would solve most of my study interruptions. My initial plan was to do a 25-minute work block with the phone out of reach, then take a five-minute break. I tried this for three morning sessions. I wrote down fewer phone checks in those sessions, but I did not measure total work completed or compare the sessions with a similar week. This note records an attempt and an early interpretation, not evidence that the phone was the main cause of lost time.

The biggest unresolved question was what happened when I sat down without a clear next action. I sometimes spent the first ten minutes deciding which problem to start. I planned to test that separately. A later note, `life-focus-correction-2026-07-04`, revises my explanation; the drawer plan remains here as history.

evidence.title: 2026-07-04-focus-correction
evidence.quote:
# Correction: starting friction, July 4

I revisited the June phone-drawer idea after four library sessions. On two days I hid the phone but still lost time deciding what to do. On the other two days I wrote a single next action before the session, such as “solve question 3 without notes,” and began sooner even though the phone stayed on the desk. These are informal observations with several changing conditions; they do not prove that next-action planning caused the improvement.

My corrected working belief is that an unclear first task may have mattered more than access to the phone in this small set of sessions. I no longer describe the drawer as the complete solution. I want to combine a written next action with reduced notifications, then compare several sessions using the same start-time measure. The older note is superseded as advice but should remain readable as the original attempt.

evidence.title: 2026-09-05-practice-plan
evidence.quote:
# Practice plan, September 5

To check whether I learned the rectangle correction, I will solve three new perimeter-and-area problems without looking at the worked solution. For each one I will write the constraint, expand the area formula, differentiate it, check the critical point and endpoints, and verify the units. I will ask for feedback on any step I cannot explain.

This is a practice plan. This vault does not contain completed practice attempts, grades, or a later test score. The September 3 note explains the corrected math, while this note records what I decided to try next. A future memory should add the outcome instead of quietly treating this plan as success.
